text: A script that always does the same thing isn't very useful. Control flow is how a script makes decisions and repeats work instead of running the exact same way every time — today covers if and else, the crucial difference between loose and strict equality, switch as a cleaner alternative, and the two loop forms you'll actually use.

if and else branch based on a condition — here, whether a balance is greater than zero. Only one branch ever runs. For comparing values, always use triple equals, not double. Double equals quietly converts types before comparing, so the string "5" double-equals the number 5 comes back true, which looks like a bug. Triple equals compares value and type with no conversion — this course uses it exclusively, so treat double equals as a footgun to avoid, not a shortcut.

When you're checking one variable against several fixed possibilities — like which network you're connected to — switch reads more clearly than a long if, else-if, else-if chain. Each case needs a break statement, or execution falls through into the next case whether you meant it to or not. A default case catches anything that doesn't match.

Use a for loop when you know how many times you want to repeat something, like looping over a fixed range of blocks. Use a while loop when you're repeating until some condition becomes false and you don't know the count in advance — like retrying a failed network request until it finally succeeds.

You're ready for lesson five when you can write an if/else that checks a condition with triple equals, and explain when you'd reach for a for loop instead of a while loop. If/else for decisions, triple equals for comparisons, switch for many possibilities against one value, for and while for repetition. Next up: functions — bundling this logic into something reusable.
